pages.text:
*Days without rain: 119. Buckets from the spring: 7.*

Yun uncurled slowly, his long sea-green body stretching out across the cracked mud until it looked like a green ribbon dropped in a dusty yard. He looked at the children, then at the flat rock beside his nose. With one careful claw, he dragged a line through the dust, smoothing it down like he was erasing a mistake.

"Before I explain," he said, his voice trembling, "you must see the list. It is very important."

Tao leaned forward, his yellow boots squeaking against the dry earth. "What kind of list?"

"Things That Could Go Wrong," Yun said.

He showed them. The writing was neat, small, and terrified.

1. Thunder.
2. Everyone hears it.
3. Everyone screams.
4. Someone cries.
5. It is my fault.

The list continued onto a second rock, then a third. The numbers climbed high into the dust, a ladder of worries leading nowhere. Mei stared at the first line. It looked familiar. It looked like the silence in her chest before she opened her mouth, that heavy, white space that waits for her to fill it.

pages.text:
"It started a long time ago," Yun said, his whiskers drooping toward the cracked mud. "I was young, rising over the village for the first time. I was very proud, and also very nervous."

He paused, studying his claws with the intensity of a student checking homework.

"My first thunder was louder than I intended. Much louder."

He did not look up. He did not blink.

"Doors banged," he listed, his voice flat and careful. "A baby howled. The ducks ran. And every single villager covered their ears and ran inside."

Mist curled around his neck like a grey scarf.

"Nobody came out to look," he said. "They stayed inside. They stayed very still. They were afraid of me."

Tao opened his mouth to ask a question, but Mei held up a hand. The silence around the pool felt thick, like cold porridge that refuses to stir.

pages.text:
"Did anyone get hurt?" Hua asked. Her voice was steady, but her fingers were white where they gripped the strap of her bag.

"No," Yun said. He tucked a claw beneath his chin. "But I did not stay to find out."

He shook his head, a slow, sad motion that made his antlers sway in the mist.

"I had never seen anything so horrible as all those faces turned toward me in fear. I hid in the pool that night. I made myself a promise."

He looked at Mei, his amber eyes wide and wet.

"I promised I would never thunder again. Not once. Not ever. It was the only way to keep them safe. It was the only way to keep myself safe."

The silence in the pool was heavy. It felt like the air before a storm that never breaks. Tao sat on a flat rock, his yellow rain boots squeaking softly against the dry stone as he shifted his weight. He looked at the dragon, then at Mei, waiting for her to say something, but Mei only watched the pearl under Yun’s chin. It was grey and heavy, pulsing faintly with the rain he held inside.

pages.text:
"But the rain does not go away," Yun said. He lifted his chin, showing them the pearl beneath it.

It was no longer just grey. It had grown dark and swollen, pulsing with a slow, wet beat. It looked like a water balloon held tight in a fist, the skin stretched thin over a liquid that wanted out.

"It stays in," he whispered. "And it gets heavier. And heavier. I have held this for a hundred years. It aches. All the time. It is like swallowing a stone and never being able to cough it up."

He gestured with a long, slender claw to the cracked edges of the pool, where the mud was dusting into the air.

"The pool is shrinking because there is no cloud to fill it. The more I hold it, the harder it is to let go. The rain is waiting for me, and I am waiting for it to stop, and neither of us is moving."

He lowered his head until one of his antlers brushed the dry ground, leaving a faint, dark damp spot.

"I am stuck, children. I am so very stuck."

pages.text:
Mei looked at the dragon. He was enormous, kind, and trembling. She saw the way he hunched his shoulders. She saw the way he waited for the world to hurt him.

It was exactly how she felt in the middle of the classroom. Twenty people waiting. Nothing coming out.

Without deciding to, without planning it, she spoke.

"You are afraid of your own voice."

Yun stared at her. The mist stopped moving.

"Yes," he whispered. "How did you know?"

Mei pressed her thumb into her palm. One. Two. Three.

"Because so am I," she said.
